title: At Key Asia Summit, Hegseth Pushes Allies to Counter China—but Stays Silent on Taiwan
summary: At the Shangri-La Dialogue, Asia's premier defense summit in Singapore, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivered a dual message: relations with China are improving, but allies must urgently ramp up military spending to counter Beijing's 'historic military buildup.' His speech, delivered just weeks after President Trump's summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, struck a more moderate tone than his 2025 address, where he accused China of seeking 'hegemonic power' and explicitly criticized harassment of Taiwan. This year, Hegseth did not mention Taiwan at all—a striking omission that sparked concern and confusion. The self-governing island, which China claims as its own, has been a flashpoint; Trump recently called arms sales to Taiwan a 'very good negotiating chip,' and a senior official later said such sales were paused due to the war in Iran. When an audience member pressed Hegseth on Taiwan, he downplayed worries, stating the U.S. had sufficient weapons stockpiled and that future sales rest solely with the president, insisting 'there has been no change in our status.' Regional experts were unimpressed. Ankit Panda of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, who attended the speech, said it was 'really light on substance,' leaving key questions unanswered. The ambiguity underscores the precarious position of smaller Southeast Asian nations, which feel squeezed between the two superpowers. Vietnam's President To Lam, in his keynote, warned that 'unchecked competition' where 'might makes it right' poses a grave risk. Hegseth also addressed the Middle East, reiterating Trump's stance that the U.S. would resume strikes on Iran if no nuclear deal is reached. China, for the second consecutive year, did not send its defense minister, opting for a lower-level delegation of military scholars. Zhou Bo, a retired Chinese air force colonel, noted Hegseth's speech was 'more moderate' and welcomed his reiteration of a 'constructive, strategic partnership' agreed upon by Trump and Xi. Yet the long-term strategic rivalry remains, and the pathway to avoiding conflict, as Panda noted, 'remains entirely unclear,' especially when the speech leaned into themes of 'lethality' and 'dominance.'
why_it_matters: The speech reflects the ongoing tension between the U.S. and China, which affects global stability and trade, and the uncertainty over Taiwan could lead to future conflicts that impact everyone.

background_read: The Shangri-La Dialogue is an annual security forum held in Singapore, organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), where defense officials from Asia and beyond discuss regional security.
Pete Hegseth is the U.S. Secretary of Defense under President Trump (since 2025).

The U.S. has long maintained a policy of strategic ambiguity regarding Taiwan (a self-governing island that China claims as its own), but recent actions by Trump—like pausing arms sales—have raised concerns among allies.
China's absence of its defense minister for two consecutive years signals its frustration with the forum's focus on tensions.
Vietnam's President To Lam (in office since 2024) has emphasized the risks of unchecked great-power competition for smaller nations.

perspectives.description: The U.S. maintains its commitment to allies while improving relations with China, potentially reducing tensions.
The ambiguity on Taiwan weakens U.S. credibility and emboldens China, while smaller nations feel squeezed.
This is part of a long-standing pattern of strategic hedging by the U.S., balancing deterrence with diplomacy.
If the U.S. continues to avoid clear commitments on Taiwan, China may test the limits, leading to a crisis.
